chapters.title: Get Modern Vim
chapters.summary: Chapter 1 is the book's installation and setup chapter: it frames the choice between Vim 8, Neovim, or running both side by side, and notes that the two editors can share the same configuration files and plugins. Tip 1 shows how to check an installed Vim's version and compiled features, then how to upgrade to Vim 8 on Debian and macOS. Tip 2 installs Neovim, explains the $VIMCONFIG/$VIMDATA convention used throughout the book, and shows how to make Neovim reuse an existing vimrc through init.vim. Tip 3 enables Neovim's Python 3 provider via the pip client, introduces providers and :checkhealth (including clipboard support), and installs neovim-remote.

chapters.title: Installing Plugins
chapters.summary: Chapter 2, Installing Plugins, explains why Vim users want plugins and how Vim 8's native packages feature removes the need for a third-party plugin manager. It defines the script/plugin/package hierarchy, shows that installing a plugin means adding it to the 'runtimepath', and demonstrates installing plugins under $VIMCONFIG/pack/{package}/start for automatic loading or under opt for on-demand loading with :packadd, plus indexing their documentation with :helptags. The chapter then covers updating plugins with git pull, migrating from Pathogen, and managing plugins with minpac (minpac#add(), minpac#update(), minpac#clean()) including user-defined commands such as :PackUpdate and :PackClean.

chapters.title: Opening Files
chapters.summary: Chapter 3 surveys ways to open files in Vim with fewer keystrokes. It first presents Junegunn Choi's fzf fuzzy finder: installation, the :FZF command and a <C-p> mapping, the picker's navigation keys, filtering noise out of the candidate list via FZF_DEFAULT_COMMAND, and reusing fzf for other sources such as buffers and command history. chapters.title: Working with the Quickfix List

chapters.title: Sessions
chapters.summary: Chapter 6 explains how Vim sessions record the current workspace, including buffers, window layout, tab pages, and cursor position, so that state can be restored after restarting Vim. It demonstrates saving with :mksession!, reloading with vim -S or :source, and automating the process with Tim Pope's Obsession plugin. It then covers persistent undo through the 'undofile' and 'undodir' options, including an autocommand that disables undo files for temporary files, and shows how Neovim terminal buffers can be renamed so their processes are restarted when a session is restored.

chapters.title: The Vim Way
chapters.summary: Chapter 1 introduces Vim's dot command as the centre of a repeatable editing workflow: it replays the last change, where a change may be a character deletion (x), a line deletion (dd), a shift (>G) or an entire Insert-mode burst. Three worked examples (Tips 2, 3 and 5) show how to craft a change worth repeating (A instead of $a, s instead of manual insertion, cw to replace a whole word) and how to make the motion repeatable too, with f{char} followed by ; or , and with * followed by n. The tips culminate in the Dot Formula - one keystroke to move, one keystroke to execute - and in the habit of reversing an over-repeated action with u or , instead of guessing.

commands.meaning: Repeat the last change
commands.evidence: The dot command lets us repeat the last change. It is the most powerful and versatile command in Vim.

commands.meaning: Delete the character under the cursor
commands.evidence: The x command deletes the character under the cursor. When we use the dot command in this context, “repeat last change” tells Vim to delete the character under the cursor:

commands.meaning: Undo the last change (restore earlier state)
commands.evidence: We can restore the file to its original state by pressing the u key a few times to undo the changes.

commands.meaning: Delete the current line as a whole
commands.evidence: The dd command also performs a deletion, but this one acts on the current line as a whole.

commands.meaning: Increase indentation from the current line to end of file
commands.evidence: Finally, the >G command increases the indentation from the current line until the end of the file. If we follow this command with the dot command, then “repeat last change” tells Vim to increase the indentation level from the current position to the end of the file. In this example, we’ll start with the cursor on the second line to highlight the difference

commands.evidence: But let’s take a closer look at this pattern: j$.. The j command moves the cursor down one line, and then the $ command moves it to the end of the line. We’ve used two keystrokes just to maneuver our cursor into position so that we can use the dot command. Do you sense that there’s room for improvement here?

commands.meaning: Append at the end of the current line (enters Insert mode)
commands.evidence: While the a command appends after the current cursor position, the A command appends at the end of the current line. It doesn’t matter where our cursor is at the time, pressing A will switch to Insert mode and move the cursor to the end of the line. In other words, it squashes $a into a single keystroke. In Two for the Price of One, we see that Vim has a handful of compound commands.

commands.meaning: Delete the character under the cursor and enter Insert mode
commands.evidence: The s command compounds two steps into one: it deletes the character under the cursor and then enters Insert mode. Having deleted the + sign, we then type + and leave Insert mode.

commands.meaning: Jump to the next occurrence of a character on the line
commands.evidence: There’s another trick in this example. The f{char} command tells Vim to look ahead for the next occurrence of the specified character and then move the cursor directly to it if a match is found (see fⓘ). So when we type f+, our cursor goes straight to the next + symbol. We’ll learn more about the f{char} command in Tip 50.

commands.meaning: Repeat the last f{char} search forward
commands.evidence: Having made our first change, we could jump to the next occurrence by repeating the f+ command, but there’s a better way. The ; command will repeat the last search that the f command performed. So instead of typing f+ four times, we can use that command once and then follow up by using the ; command three times.

commands.meaning: Repeat the last f{char} search in the reverse direction
commands.evidence: Whenever Vim makes it easy to repeat an action or a motion, it always provides some way of backing out in case we accidentally go too far. In the case of the dot command, we can always hit the u key to undo the last change. If we hit the ; key too many times after using the f{char} command, we’ll miss our mark. But we can back up again by pressing the , key, which repeats the last f{char} search in the reverse direction (see Tip 50).

commands.meaning: Substitute every occurrence of content with copy in the file
Search for the word under the cursor
commands.evidence: You might have guessed by now that the dot command is my favorite single-key Vim trigger. In second place is the * command. This executes a search for the word under the cursor at that moment (see *ⓘ).

commands.meaning: Jump to the next match of the current search
commands.evidence: Having executed a search for the word “content,” we can now advance to the next occurrence just by hitting the n key. In this case, pressing *nn would cycle through all matches, taking us back to where we started.

commands.meaning: Change to the end of the word, then enter Insert mode
commands.evidence: With our cursor positioned at the start of the word “content,” we are poised to change it. This involves two steps: deleting the word “content” and then typing its replacement. The cw command deletes to the end of the word and then drops us into Insert mode, where we can spell out the word “copy.” Vim records our keystrokes until we leave Insert mode, so the full sequence cwcopy<Esc> is considered to be a single change. Pressing the . command deletes to the end of the current word and changes it to “copy.”

chapters.title: Normal Mode
chapters.summary: Chapter 2 presents Normal mode as Vim’s natural resting state, using a painter’s brush-off-the-canvas analogy to argue that most editing time goes into thinking, navigating, and transforming text rather than inserting it. It explains how pausing to leave Insert mode at natural break points chunks the undo history, and how composing changes so that the dot command can repeat them beats a one-off efficient edit. Counts are then applied to simple arithmetic with <C-a> and <C-x>, including the leading-zero octal pitfall and the case for repeating over counting, before the chapter closes with operator+motion grammar, operator doubling, custom operators and motions, and Operator-Pending mode.

commands.meaning: Undo the most recent change; each trip into Insert mode counts as one change.
commands.evidence: The u key triggers the undo command, which reverts the most recent change. A change could be anything that modifies the text in the document. That includes commands triggered from Normal, Visual, and Command-Line modes, but a change could also encompass any text entered (or deleted) in Insert mode. So we could also say that i{insert some text}<Esc> constitutes a change.

commands.meaning: Delete backward from the cursor to the start of the current word.
commands.evidence: Pressing db deletes from the cursor’s starting position to the beginning of the word, but it leaves the final “h” intact. We can delete this rogue character by pressing x. That gives us a Vim golf score of 3.

commands.meaning: Motion that moves the cursor backward to the start of the current word.
commands.evidence: We have to start by maneuvering our cursor into position with the b motion. Once it’s in place, we can excise the word with a single dw command. Once again, our Vim golf score is 3.

commands.meaning: Delete the single character under the cursor.
commands.evidence: The backward deletion technique involves two operations: db deletes to the start of the word and then x deletes a single character. If we invoke the dot command, it repeats the single character deletion (. == x). That’s not what I would call a big win.

commands.meaning: Delete from the cursor to the start of the next word.
commands.evidence: The forward deletion technique also involves two steps. This time, b is just a plain motion, while dw makes a change. The dot command repeats dw, deleting from the cursor position to the beginning of the next word. It so happens that we’re already at the end of the line. There is no “next word,” so in this context the dot command isn’t useful. But at least it’s shorthand for something longer (. == dw).

commands.meaning: Delete a whole word plus its surrounding whitespace (delete a word).
commands.evidence: The daw command is easily remembered by the mnemonic delete a word. We’ll go into more detail on text objects in Tip 52, and Tip 53.

commands.meaning: Dot command: repeat the last change, here repeating daw on another word.
commands.evidence: The final solution only invokes a single operation: daw. This technique doesn’t just remove the word, it also deletes a whitespace character. As a result, our cursor ends up on the last character of the word “is.” If we invoke the dot command, it will repeat the instruction to delete a word. This time, the dot command does something truly useful (. == daw).

commands.meaning: Increment the number at or after the cursor; a count adds that amount.
commands.evidence: The <C-a> and <C-x> commands perform addition and subtraction on numbers. When run without a count they increment by one, but if we prefix a number, then we can add or subtract by any whole number. For example, if we positioned our cursor on a 5 character, running 10<C-a> would modify it to read 15.

commands.meaning: Yank the current line and paste it below, duplicating the line.
commands.evidence: We’re going to duplicate the last line and make two small modifications to it: replace the word “blog” with “news,” and change “0px” to “-180px.” We can duplicate the line by running yyp and then using cW to change the first word. But how should we deal with that number?

commands.meaning: Decrement by 180; with the cursor off a digit it jumps forward to the first number on the line.
commands.evidence: One approach would be to jump to the digit with f0 and then dip into Insert mode to change the value by hand: i-18<Esc>. But it’s quicker just to run 180<C-x>. Since our cursor isn’t on a digit to begin with, it jumps forward to the first one that it finds. That saves us the step of moving the cursor by hand. Let’s see this work flow in action:

commands.meaning: Count applied to the delete operator, deleting two words (same result as d2w).
commands.evidence: We can approach this in a handful of ways. Both d2w and 2dw will work. With d2w, we invoke the delete command and then give 2w as the motion. We could read that as “delete two words.” However, 2dw turns things around. This time the count applies to the delete command, but the motion acts over a single word. We could read this as “delete a word two times.” Putting semantics aside, we get the same result either way.

commands.meaning: Change three words with a count, then type the replacement text.
Combine the gU operator with the aw text object to uppercase the current word.
commands.evidence: Suppose that we already know how to delete a word using daw, and then we learn about the gU command (see gUⓘ). It’s an operator too, so we can invoke gUaw to convert the current word to SHOUTY case. If we then expand our vocabulary to include the ap motion, which acts upon a paragraph, then we find two new operations at our disposal: dap to delete, or gUap to make the whole paragraph shout.

commands.meaning: Operator invoked in duplicate acts on the current line: delete the whole line.
commands.evidence: Vim’s grammar has just one more rule: when an operator command is invoked in duplicate, it acts upon the current line. So dd deletes the current line, while >> indents it. The gU command is a special case. We can make it act upon the current line by running either gUgU or the shorthand gUU.

commands.meaning: Jump to the top of the file with gg, then =G autoindents everything to the end.
commands.evidence: If we wanted to autoindent the entire file using the = command, we could run gg=G (that is, gg to jump to the top of the file and then =G to autoindent everything from the cursor position to the end of the file). But if we had the textobj-entire plugin installed, we could simply run =ae. It wouldn’t matter where our cursor was when we ran this command; it would always act upon the entire file.

concepts.name: Normal mode as the natural resting state
concepts.evidence: Normal mode is Vim’s natural resting state. If this chapter seems surprisingly short, then that’s because most of this book is about how to use Normal mode! Here, however, is where we cover some core concepts and general tips.

concepts.name: Chunking undos by controlling undo granularity
concepts.evidence: In other text editors, invoking the undo command after typing a few words might revert the last typed word or character. However, in Vim we can control the granularity of the undo command.

concepts.name: Compose repeatable changes
concepts.evidence: Vim is optimized for repetition. In order to exploit this, we have to be mindful of how we compose our changes.

concepts.name: Investing the most power in the dot command
concepts.evidence: The daw technique invests the most power into the dot command, so I declare it the winner of this round.

concepts.name: Using counts to do simple arithmetic
concepts.evidence: Most Normal mode commands can be executed with a count. We can exploit this feature to do simple arithmetic.

concepts.name: Number formats and leading-zero octal notation
concepts.evidence: If you answered 008, then you might be in for a surprise when you try using Vim’s <C-a> command on any number with a leading zero. As is the convention in some programming languages, Vim can interpret numerals with a leading zero to be in octal notation rather than in decimal. In the octal numeric system, 007 + 001 = 010, which looks like the decimal ten but is actually an octal eight. Confused?

concepts.name: Prefer repeating over counting
concepts.evidence: Counting is tedious. I’d rather hit the dot command six times than spend the same time looking ahead in order to reduce the number of keys that I have to press. What if I hit the dot command one too many times? No matter, I just back up by hitting the u key once.

concepts.name: Act, repeat, reverse
concepts.evidence: Remember our mantra (from Tip 4): act, repeat, reverse. Here it is in action.

concepts.name: Operator + motion = action
concepts.evidence: The d{motion} command can operate on a single character (dl), a complete word (daw), or an entire paragraph (dap). Its reach is defined by the motion. The same goes for c{motion}, y{motion}, and a handful of others. Collectively, these commands are called operators. You can find the complete list by looking up operatorⓘ, while Table 2, Vim’s Operator Commands, summarizes some of the more common ones.

concepts.name: Vim’s operator-motion grammar
concepts.evidence: The combination of operators with motions forms a kind of grammar. The first rule is simple: an action is composed from an operator followed by a motion. Learning new motions and operators is like learning the vocabulary of Vim. If we follow the simple grammar rules, we can express more ideas as our vocabulary grows.

concepts.name: Operator doubling acts on the current line
concepts.evidence: Vim’s grammar has just one more rule: when an operator command is invoked in duplicate, it acts upon the current line. So dd deletes the current line, while >> indents it. The gU command is a special case. We can make it act upon the current line by running either gUgU or the shorthand gUU.

concepts.name: Operator-Pending mode
concepts.evidence: If we think of Vim as a finite-state machine, then Operator-Pending mode is a state that accepts only motion commands. It is activated when we invoke an operator command, and then nothing happens until we provide a motion, which completes the operation. While Operator-Pending mode is active, we can return to Normal mode in the usual manner by pressing escape, which aborts the operation.

chapters.title: Insert Mode
chapters.summary: Chapter 3, Insert Mode, covers the operations Vim makes available while you are already inserting text. It starts with fast self-corrections using <C-h>, <C-w>, and <C-u>, then shows the shortcuts for returning to Normal mode and Insert Normal mode (<C-o>) for running a single Normal command. The middle tips explain pasting register contents without leaving Insert mode and using the expression register for in-place calculations. The chapter ends with inserting unusual characters by numeric code or digraph, and with Replace and Virtual Replace modes for overwriting existing text.

commands.meaning: Delete back one character (backspace) while staying in Insert mode
Delete back one word
Delete back to start of line
Switch to Normal mode
Switch to Normal mode; synonymous with <Esc>
Switch to Insert Normal mode to run one Normal command, then return to Insert mode
Insert the contents of the named register at the cursor without leaving Insert mode
commands.evidence: The general format of the command is <C-r>{register}, where {register} is the address of the register we want to insert (see i_CTRL-Rⓘ).

commands.meaning: Insert register text literally and fix unintended indentation
commands.evidence: The <C-r><C-p>{register} command is smarter. It inserts text literally and fixes any unintended indentation (see i_CTRL-R_CTRL-Pⓘ). But it’s a bit of a handful! If I want to paste a register containing multiple lines of text, I prefer to switch to Normal mode and use one of the put commands (see Tip 63).

commands.meaning: Open the expression-register prompt from Insert mode; <CR> inserts the evaluated result
commands.evidence: The expression register is addressed by the = symbol. From Insert mode we can access it by typing <C-r>=. This opens a prompt at the bottom of the screen where we can type the expression that we want to evaluate. When done, we hit <CR>, and Vim inserts the result at our current position in the document.

commands.meaning: Insert an arbitrary character by its three-digit decimal code
commands.evidence: We can tell Vim to insert any arbitrary character if we know its numeric code. From Insert mode, we just have to type <C-v>{code}, where {code} is the address of the character that we want to insert.

commands.meaning: Insert a character by four-digit hexadecimal code, for example <C-v>u00bf for the inverted question mark
commands.evidence: But what if we wanted to insert a character whose numeric code is longer than three digits? For example, the Unicode Basic Multilingual Plane has an address space for up to 65,535 characters. It turns out that we can enter all of these using a four-digit hexadecimal code if we type <C-v>u{1234} (note the u preceding the digit this time). Let’s say we wanted to insert an inverted question mark symbol (“¿”), which is represented by the character code 00bf. From Insert mode, we would just have to type <C-v>u00bf. See i_CTRL-V_digitⓘ for more details.

commands.meaning: Insert the character represented by a two-character digraph, for example <C-k>?I
commands.evidence: Digraphs are easy to use. From Insert mode, we just type <C-k>{char1}{char2}. So if we wanted to insert the “¿” character, which is represented by the digraph ?I, we would simply type <C-k>?I.

commands.meaning: Enter Replace mode, which overwrites existing text until <Esc>
commands.evidence: From Normal mode, we can engage Replace mode with the R command. As the example demonstrates, typing “, b” overwrites the existing “. B” characters. And when we’re finished with Replace mode, we can hit the <Esc> key to return to Normal mode. Not all keyboards have an <Insert> key, but if yours does, then you can use it to toggle between Insert and Replace modes.

commands.meaning: Enter Virtual Replace mode, which overwrites screen columns and treats a tab as spaces
commands.evidence: Vim has a second variant of Replace mode. Virtual Replace mode is triggered with gR and treats the tab character as though it consisted of spaces. Suppose that we position the cursor on a tab stop spanning eight columns of screen real estate. If we switch to Virtual Replace mode, we could type up to seven characters, each of which would be inserted in front of the tab character. Finally, if we typed an eighth character, it would replace the tab stop.

commands.meaning: Single-shot replace: overwrite one character (or one virtual character) and return to Normal mode
commands.evidence: Vim also provides a single-shot version of Replace mode and Virtual Replace mode. The r{char} and gr{char} commands allow us to overwrite a single character before switching straight back to Normal mode (rⓘ).

concepts.name: Immediate correction from Insert mode
concepts.evidence: If we make a mistake while composing text in Insert mode, we can fix it immediately. There’s no need to change modes. Besides the backspace key, we can use a couple of other Insert mode commands to make quick corrections.

concepts.name: Insert Normal mode
concepts.evidence: Insert Normal mode is a special version of Normal mode, which gives us one bullet. We can fire off a single command, after which we’ll be returned to Insert mode immediately. From Insert mode, we can switch to Insert Normal mode by pressing <C-o> (i_CTRL-Oⓘ).

concepts.name: Pasting from a register without leaving Insert mode
concepts.evidence: Vim’s yank and put operations are usually executed from Normal mode, but sometimes we might want to paste text into the document without leaving Insert mode.

concepts.name: Expression register
concepts.evidence: The expression register is different. It can evaluate a piece of Vim script code and return the result. Here, we can use it like a calculator. Passing it a simple arithmetic expression, such as 1+1, gives a result of 2. We can use the return value from the expression register just as though it were a piece of text saved in a plain old register.

concepts.name: Character insertion by numeric code
concepts.evidence: Vim can insert any character by its numeric code. This can be handy for entering symbols that are not found on the keyboard.

concepts.name: Digraph insertion
concepts.evidence: While Vim allows us to insert any character by its numeric code, these can be hard to remember and awkward to type. We can also insert unusual characters as digraphs: pairs of characters that are easy to remember.

concepts.name: Replace mode
concepts.evidence: Replace mode is identical to Insert mode, except that it overwrites existing text in the document.

concepts.name: Virtual Replace mode
concepts.evidence: In Virtual Replace mode, we overwrite characters of screen real estate rather than dealing with the actual characters that would eventually be saved in a file. This tends to produce fewer surprises, so I would recommend using Virtual Replace mode whenever possible.

concepts.name: Single-shot replace commands
concepts.evidence: Vim also provides a single-shot version of Replace mode and Virtual Replace mode. The r{char} and gr{char} commands allow us to overwrite a single character before switching straight back to Normal mode (rⓘ).

concepts.name: Caps Lock remapping
concepts.evidence: Many Vim users remap the Caps Lock button to make it act like another key, such as <Esc> or <Ctrl>. On modern keyboards, the <Esc> key is difficult to reach, whereas the Caps Lock key is handy. Mapping Caps Lock to behave as an <Esc> key can save a lot of effort, especially since the <Esc> key is so heavily used in Vim. I prefer to map the Caps Lock button to behave instead as a <Ctrl> key. The <C-[> mapping is synonymous with <Esc>, and it’s easier to type when the <Ctrl> key is within easy reach. Additionally, the <Ctrl> key can be used for many other mappings, both in Vim and in other programs too.

concepts.name: Register-paste side effects under 'textwidth' and 'autoindent'
concepts.evidence: The <C-r>{register} command is convenient for pasting a few words from Insert mode. If the register contains a lot of text, you might notice a slight delay before the screen updates. That’s because Vim inserts the text from the register as if it were being typed one character at a time. If the ‘textwidth’ or ‘autoindent’ options are enabled, you might end up with unwanted line breaks or extra indentation.

concepts.name: Literal insertion of a following key with <C-v>
concepts.evidence: In another scenario, if the <C-v> command is followed by any nondigit key, it will insert the character represented by that key literally. For example, if the ‘expandtab’ option is enabled, then pressing the <Tab> key will insert space characters instead of a tab character. However, pressing <C-v><Tab> will always insert a tab character literally, regardless of whether ‘expandtab’ is enabled or not.

chapters.title: Visual Mode
chapters.summary: Chapter 4 introduces Visual mode as a way to define a selection and then operate on it, covering the character-wise, line-wise, and block-wise submodes, how to enable and switch between them, and the gv and o keys for reselecting and flipping the free end of a selection. It shows that Visual commands can be repeated with the dot command, but that the dot command replays the same amount of text, so line-wise selections repeat reliably while character-wise ones fall short, making Normal-mode operators such as gU{motion} preferable for repetitive edits. The chapter closes with Visual-Block techniques for editing tabular data, inserting text into several lines at once, and appending after a ragged block whose lines have different lengths.

commands.meaning: Enable character-wise Visual mode from Normal mode
commands.evidence: The v key is our gateway into Visual mode. From Normal mode, we can press v by itself to enable character-wise Visual mode. Line-wise Visual mode is enabled by pressing V (with the Shift key), and block-wise Visual mode by pressing <C-v> (with the Control key). These commands are summarized in the following table:

commands.meaning: Enable line-wise Visual mode (Shift-v)
Enable block-wise Visual mode (Ctrl-v)
Reselect the last visual selection, whatever its submode
commands.evidence: The gv command is a useful little shortcut. It reselects the range of text that was last selected in Visual mode. No matter whether the previous selection was character-wise, line-wise, or block-wise, the gv command should do the right thing. The only case where it might get confused is if the last selection has since been deleted.

commands.meaning: Switch to the other (free) end of the selection so its bounds can be redefined
commands.evidence: The range of a Visual mode selection is marked by two ends: one end is fixed and the other moves freely with our cursor. We can use the o key to toggle the free end. This is really handy if halfway through defining a selection we realize that we started in the wrong place. Rather than leaving Visual mode and starting afresh, we can just hit o and redefine the bounds of the selection. The following demonstrates how we can use this technique:

commands.meaning: Toggle between Visual and Select modes
commands.evidence: We can toggle between Visual and Select modes by pressing <C-g>. The only visible difference is the message at the bottom of screen, which switches between -- VISUAL -- and -- SELECT --. But if we type any printable character in Select mode, it will replace the selection and switch to Insert mode. Of course, from Visual mode you could just as well use the c key to change the selection.

commands.meaning: Visually select the word under the cursor
commands.evidence: Let’s revisit the simple example where we wanted to change the word “March” to “April.” This time, suppose that we have left the confines of the text area on a web page and we’re comfortably back inside Vim. We place our cursor somewhere on the word “March” and run viw to visually select the word. Now, we can’t just type the word “April” because that would trigger the A command and append the text “pril”! Instead, we’ll use the c command to change the selection, deleting the word and dropping us into Insert mode, where we can type out the word “April” in full. This pattern of usage is similar to our original example, except that we use the c key instead of backspace.

commands.meaning: Visually select the inner contents of the current tag (text object)
commands.evidence: We can select the inner contents of a tag by running vit, which can be read as: visually select inside the tag. The it command is a special kind of motion called a text object, which we’ll cover in detail in Tip 52.

commands.meaning: Convert the selected characters to uppercase
commands.evidence: In Visual mode, we make a selection and then act on it. In this case, we could use the U command, which converts the selected characters to uppercase (v_Uⓘ). See Table 4, Uppercasing in Visual Mode.

commands.meaning: Normal-mode operator that uppercases the text covered by a motion
commands.evidence: The Visual mode U command has a Normal mode equivalent: gU{motion} (gUⓘ). If we use this to make the first change, we can complete the subsequent edits using the Dot Formula:

commands.meaning: Move down one line and repeat the last change with the dot command (Dot Formula)
commands.evidence: Running j. advances our cursor to the next line and then repeats the last change. It works fine on line two, but if we try it again we end up with this strange-looking result:

commands.meaning: Indent the selected range by one level
commands.evidence: In our malformed Python excerpt, the two lines below the while keyword should be indented further by two levels. We could fix it by visually selecting the text and triggering the > command to indent it. But that would only increase the indentation by one level before dropping us back into Normal mode.

commands.meaning: Delete the selected column in Visual-Block mode
commands.evidence: To begin, we use <C-v> to engage Visual-Block mode; then we define the column selection by moving our cursor down several lines. Pressing the x key deletes that column, and the dot command repeats the deletion for the same range of text. We repeat until the two columns are about the right distance apart.

commands.meaning: Replace every character in the selection with a pipe character
commands.evidence: Now that we’ve lined up the two columns of text where we want them, we’re ready to draw a line between them. We can reselect our last visual selection using the gv command and then press r| to replace each character in the selection with a pipe character.

commands.meaning: Append text at the end of each line of a Visual-Block selection
commands.evidence: Having defined our selection, we can append at the end of each line using the A command (see Vim’s Conventions for “i” and “a” Keys). This drops us into Insert mode on the topmost line of our selection. Anything that we type will appear on this line only for the duration of Insert mode, but as soon as we revert to Normal mode, our changes are propagated across the rest of the lines that we selected.

concepts.name: Visual mode's three submodes
concepts.evidence: Vim has three kinds of Visual mode. In character-wise Visual mode, we can select anything from a single character up to a range of characters within a line or spanning multiple lines. This is suitable for working at the level of individual words or phrases. If we want to operate on entire lines, we can use line-wise Visual mode instead. Finally, block-wise Visual mode allows us to work with columnar regions of the document. Block-wise Visual mode is quite special, so we’ll discuss it at greater length in Tip 24, Tip 25, and Tip 26.

concepts.name: Inversion of control: operator-then-range versus selection-then-command
concepts.evidence: Some Visual mode commands perform the same basic function as in Normal mode but with a slight twist. For example, the c command is consistent in both modes in that it deletes the specified text and then switches to Insert mode. The difference is in how we specify the range on which to act. From Normal mode, we trigger the change command first and then specify the range as a motion. This, if you’ll remember from Tip 12, is called an operator command. Whereas in Visual mode, we start off by making the selection and then trigger the change command. This inversion of control can be generalized for all operator commands (see Table 2, Vim’s Operator Commands). For most people, the Visual mode approach feels more intuitive.

concepts.name: Select mode
concepts.evidence: In a typical text editing environment, selected text is deleted when we type any printable character. Vim’s Visual mode doesn’t follow this convention—but Select mode does. According to Vim’s built-in documentation, it “resembles the selection mode in Microsoft Windows” (see Select-modeⓘ). Printable characters cause the selection to be deleted, Vim enters Insert mode, and the typed character is inserted.

concepts.name: Toggling the free end of a selection
concepts.evidence: Toggling the Free End of a Selection

concepts.name: Repeating line-wise Visual commands with the dot command
concepts.evidence: When we use the dot command to repeat a change made to a visual selection, it repeats the change on the same range of text. In this tip, we’ll make a change to a line-wise selection and then repeat it with the dot command.

concepts.name: Dot Formula
concepts.evidence: Having transformed the first line, we now want to perform the same change on the next two lines. How about we try using the Dot Formula?

concepts.name: Visual-command repeat replays the same range of text
concepts.evidence: Do you see what’s happened? When a Visual mode command is repeated, it affects the same range of text (see visual-repeatⓘ). In this case, the original command affected a word consisting of three letters. This works fine for line two, which happens to also contain a three-letter word, but it falls short when we try to repeat the command on a word containing five letters.

concepts.name: Preferring operators to Visual commands where possible
concepts.evidence: If we want to set up the dot command so that it repeats something useful, then we’re better off staying out of Visual mode. As a general rule, we should prefer operator commands over their Visual mode equivalents when working through a repetitive set of changes.

concepts.name: Text objects (it means inside the tag)
concepts.evidence: We can select the inner contents of a tag by running vit, which can be read as: visually select inside the tag. The it command is a special kind of motion called a text object, which we’ll cover in detail in Tip 52.

concepts.name: Using Visual-Block mode on tabular data
concepts.evidence: We can work with rows of text in any editor, but manipulating columns of text requires a more specialized tool. Vim provides this capability in the form of its Visual-Block mode, which we’ll use to transform a plain-text table.

concepts.name: Inserting text into several lines with a block change
concepts.evidence: We can use Visual-Block mode to insert text into several lines of text simultaneously.

concepts.name: Ragged Visual Block selection to the end of unequal lines
concepts.evidence: After engaging Visual-Block mode, we extend our selection to the end of each line by pressing $. At first glance, one might expect this to cause difficulty because each line is a different length. But in this context, Vim understands that we want to extend our selection to the end of all selected lines. This lets us break free from our rectangular constraints, creating a selection that traces the ragged right edge of our text.

chapters.title: Command-Line Mode
chapters.summary: Chapter 5 explains Command-Line mode and the Ex commands it exposes, opening with a catalog of Ex commands that operate on buffer text and the control-key chords available at the prompt. It shows how to build [range] addresses from line numbers, marks, and patterns, and how to duplicate or move lines with :copy/:t and :move/:m. Later tips cover running Normal mode commands across a range with :normal, repeating Ex commands with @:, tab-completion and wildmode, inserting the word under the cursor with <C-r><C-w>, and recalling history in the command-line window. The final tips cover running shell commands and filtering ranges through external programs, then batching Ex commands in a script and sourcing it across the argument list.

commands.meaning: Print lines 2 through 5, using line-number addresses for the range.
Replace the first occurrence of Practical with Pragmatic on every line of the file.
Print the lines covered by the most recent Visual-mode selection.
Print the range from the opening <html> tag to the closing </html> tag, using pattern addresses.
Print that same block without its first and last lines, using offset addresses.
Duplicate the current line below itself without using a register.
Append a semicolon at the end of every line by running a Normal mode command across a range.
Repeat the most recently executed Ex command.
commands.evidence: In Chapter 1, The Vim Way, we saw how the . command can be used to repeat the last change. But the dot command won’t replay changes made from Vim’s command line. Instead, we can repeat the last Ex command by pressing @: (see @:ⓘ).

commands.meaning: Reveal the list of possible tab-completions for the col prefix.
Insert the word under the cursor at the command-line prompt.
commands.evidence: At Vim’s command line, the <C-r><C-w> mapping copies the word under the cursor and inserts it at the command-line prompt. We can use this to save ourselves a bit of typing.

commands.meaning: Open the command-line window with the history of Ex commands.
commands.evidence: Each of these commands is already in our history, so we shouldn’t have to type the entire command line from scratch. But how can we merge two records from our history into one? Press q: and meet the command-line window (see cmdwinⓘ).

commands.meaning: Run an external command, with % standing for the current file name.
Filter lines 2 through the last line through the external sort command.
Run :join on every line where href matches (global command).
Source the script once in every file of the argument list.

concepts.name: Ex commands strike far and wide
concepts.evidence: As a general rule, we could say that Ex commands are long range and have the capacity to modify many lines in a single move. Or to condense that even further: Ex commands strike far and wide.

concepts.name: Range syntax {start},{end}
concepts.evidence: :{start},{end}

concepts.name: Visual selection range marks
concepts.evidence: ’< is a mark standing for the first line of the visual selection, while ’> is the last line of the visual selection (see Tip 54, for more about marks). These marks persist even when we leave Visual mode. If you try running :’<,’>p straight from Normal mode, it will always act on the lines that most recently formed a Visual mode selection.

concepts.name: Pattern addresses in a range
concepts.evidence: This looks quite complex, but it follows the usual form for a range: :{start},{end}. The {start} address in this case is the pattern /<html>/, while the {end} address is /<\/html>/. In other words, the range begins on the line containing an opening <html> tag and ends on the line containing the corresponding closing tag.

concepts.name: Address symbols for ranges
concepts.evidence: The syntax for defining a range is very flexible. We can mix and match line numbers, marks, and patterns, and we can apply an offset to any of them. This table summarizes a few of the symbols that can be used to create addresses and ranges for Ex commands:

concepts.name: :t as the copy TO mnemonic
concepts.evidence: We could shorten the :copy command to only two letters, as :co. Or we can be even more succinct by using the :t command, which is a synonym for :copy. As a mnemonic, you can think of it as copy TO. This table shows a few examples of the :t command in action:

concepts.name: Moving lines with :m
concepts.evidence: We can shorten it to a single letter: :m. Suppose that we want to move the Hardware Store section after the Beauty Parlor section. We could do so using the :move command as shown in Table 8, Moving a Set of Lines with the ‘:m’ Command.

concepts.name: The : register and @: repeat
concepts.evidence: Then we use @: to repeat the command. Note the similarity between this and the method for executing a macro (Play Back a Sequence of Commands by Executing a Macro). Also note that the : register always holds the most recently executed command line (see quote_:ⓘ). After running @: for the first time, we can subsequently repeat it with the @@ command.

concepts.name: wildmode and wildmenu completion
concepts.evidence: We can customize this behavior by tweaking the ‘wildmode’ option (see 'wildmode'ⓘ). If you’re used to working with the bash shell, then this setting will match your expectations:

concepts.name: Command-line window
concepts.evidence: The command-line window is like a regular Vim buffer, where each line contains an item from our history. With the k and j keys, we can move backward and forward through our history. Or we can use Vim’s search feature to find the line that we’re looking for. When we press the <CR> key, the contents of the current line are executed as an Ex command.

concepts.name: Filtering a range through an external program
concepts.evidence: The :!{cmd} command takes on a different meaning when it’s given a range. The lines specified by [range] are passed as standard input for the {cmd}, and then the output from {cmd} overwrites the original contents of [range]. Or to put it another way, the [range] is filtered through the specified {cmd} (see :range!ⓘ). Vim defines a filter as “a program that accepts text as standard input, changes it in some way, and sends it to standard output.”

concepts.name: Batching Ex commands in a sourced script
concepts.evidence: We can use the :source command to execute the batch.vim script (see sourceⓘ).

chapters.title: Manage Multiple Files
chapters.summary: Chapter 6 explains how Vim manages multiple files through the buffer list, the argument list, and split windows organized into tab pages. It distinguishes files on disk from in-memory buffers, shows how to inspect and navigate the buffer list with :ls, :bnext, and <C-^>, and warns about hiding modified buffers and reconciling them when quitting. It then covers populating the :args argument list with names, globs, and backtick expansion, running :argdo across that set, and finally dividing the workspace with <C-w>s and <C-w>v, moving focus, resizing, and using :tabedit with {N}gt to switch tab pages.

commands.meaning: List all loaded buffers with their numbers and status flags.
Switch to the next buffer in the buffer list.
Toggle between the current buffer and the alternate file.
commands.evidence: The % symbol indicates which of the buffers is visible in the current window, while the # symbol represents the alternate file. We can quickly toggle between the current and alternate files by pressing <C-^>. Press it once, and we’ll switch to a.txt; press it a second time, and we’ll get back to b.txt.

commands.meaning: Jump directly to a buffer by number, or by a unique fragment of its name.
commands.evidence: The :ls listing starts with a digit, which is assigned to each buffer automatically on creation. We can jump directly to a buffer by number, using the :buffer N command (see :bⓘ). Alternatively, we can use the more intuitive form, :buffer {bufname}. The {bufname} need only contain enough characters from the filepath to uniquely identify the buffer. If we enter a string that matches more than one of the items in the buffer list, we can use tab-completion to choose between the options (see Tip 32).

It explains how :edit resolves filepaths against the working directory or the active buffer's directory (using %:h), how to configure 'path' and use :find to open files by name, and how the netrw plugin's :Explore commands browse directories. chapters.title: Navigate Inside Files with Motions
chapters.summary: Chapter 8 is a tour of motions for moving within a file. It starts with home-row h/j/k/l and the difference between real lines and display lines (j/k vs. gj/gk, 0/^/$ and their g variants), then covers word and WORD motions (w/b/e/ge, W/B/E/gE), character searches (f/F/t/T with ; and ,), and the search command (/pattern with n and N), including its use as an operator motion. The chapter ends with text objects (i/a prefixes, iw/aw, daw/ciw), marks (m, `{mark}, automatic marks), % with the matchit plugin, and a brief look at surround.vim.

These commands allow us to traverse Vim’s jump list, but what exactly is a jump?

concepts.evidence: In web browsers, we’re used to using the back button to return to pages that we visited earlier. chapters.title: Copy and Paste
chapters.summary: Chapter 10 explains Vim's copy-and-paste model, where delete cuts into registers, yank copies, and put pastes. It walks through transposing characters with xp, transposing lines with ddp, and duplicating lines with yyp, then shows the "clobbered yank" pitfall in which diw overwrites the unnamed register. Tip 61 catalogues the register types: unnamed (""), yank ("0), named ("a-"z), black hole ("_), system clipboard ("+) and selection ("*), plus the expression ("=) and read-only registers. Tips 62-64 cover replacing a Visual selection with a register (and its content-swapping side effect), line-wise versus character-wise put behavior with gP and <C-r>{register}, and avoiding autoindent corruption from the system paste command by using the 'paste' and 'pastetoggle' options.

concepts.name: Delete, yank, and put terminology
concepts.evidence: Vim’s delete command is equivalent to the standard cut operation. That is, it copies the specified text into a register and then removes it from the document. Understanding this is key to avoiding the common pitfall outlined in Oops! I Clobbered My Yank.

concepts.name: The unnamed register
concepts.evidence: If we don’t specify which register we want to interact with, then Vim will use the unnamed register, which is addressed by the " symbol (see quote_quoteⓘ). To address this register explicitly, we have to use two double quote marks: for example, ""p, which is effectively equivalent to p by itself.

concepts.name: The yank register
concepts.evidence: When we use the y{motion} command, the specified text is copied not only into the unnamed register but also into the yank register, which is addressed by the 0 symbol (see quote0ⓘ).

concepts.name: The named registers
concepts.evidence: Vim has one named register for each letter of the alphabet (see quote_alphaⓘ). That means that we can cut ("ad{motion}), copy ("ay{motion}), or paste ("ap) up to twenty-six pieces of text.

concepts.name: The black hole register
concepts.evidence: The black hole register is a place from which nothing returns. It’s addressed by the underscore symbol (see quote_ⓘ). If we run the command "_d{motion}, then Vim deletes the specified text without saving a copy of it. This can be useful if we want to delete text without overwriting the contents of the unnamed register.

concepts.name: The system clipboard (plus) register
concepts.evidence: Vim’s plus register references the system clipboard and is addressed by the + symbol (see quote+ⓘ).

concepts.name: The selection (star) register and the X11 primary clipboard
concepts.evidence: The X11 windowing system has a second kind of clipboard called the primary. This represents the most recently selected text, and we can use the middle mouse button (if we have one) to paste from it. Vim’s quotestar register maps to the primary clipboard and is addressed by the * symbol (quotestarⓘ).

concepts.name: The expression register
concepts.evidence: Vim’s registers can be thought of simply as containers that hold a block of text. The expression register, referenced by the = symbol (quote=ⓘ), is an exception. When we fetch the contents of the expression register, Vim drops into Command-Line mode, showing an = prompt. We can enter a Vim script expression and then press <CR> to execute it. If the expression returns a string (or a value that can be easily coerced into a string), then Vim uses it.

concepts.name: Read-only registers
concepts.evidence: We can set the contents of the named, unnamed, and yank registers explicitly using the delete and yank commands. In addition, Vim provides a handful of registers whose values are set implicitly. These are known collectively as the read-only registers (quote.ⓘ). The following table summarizes them:

concepts.name: Visual put swaps text with the register
concepts.evidence: Think of it this way: the visual selection in the document swaps places with the text in the register. Is it a feature? Is it a bug? You decide!

concepts.name: Line-wise vs. character-wise registers
concepts.evidence: Whether the p command puts the text from the register after the current character or after the current line depends on how the specified register was set. A line-wise yank or delete operation (such as dd, yy, or dap) creates a line-wise register, whereas a character-wise yank or delete (such as x, diw, or das) creates a character-wise register. In general, the outcome of using the p command is fairly intuitive (see linewise-registerⓘ for more details).

concepts.name: The 'paste' option for pasting in a terminal
concepts.evidence: GVim is able to discern when text is pasted from the clipboard and adjust its behavior accordingly, but when Vim runs inside a terminal this information is not available. The ‘paste’ option allows us to manually warn Vim that we’re about to use the system paste command. When the ‘paste’ option is enabled, Vim turns off all Insert mode mappings and abbreviations and resets a host of options, including ‘autoindent’ (look up 'paste'ⓘ for the full list). That allows us to safely paste from the system clipboard with no surprises.

chapters.title: Macros
chapters.summary: Chapter 11 introduces Vim macros: recording keystrokes into a register with q{register} and replaying them with @{register} or @@. It contrasts executing a macro in series, where one failure aborts the remaining queued repetitions, with executing it in parallel via :normal @a or :argdo normal @a, where each invocation is independent. It also teaches repeatable macro design (normalize the cursor, prefer robust motions, let failed motions abort safely), playback with a count, appending with qA, editing a macro as plain text, and using the expression register with a counter to number list items.

commands.meaning: Begin recording keystrokes into the named register
commands.evidence: The q key functions both as the “record” button and the “stop” button. To begin recording our keystrokes, we type q{register}, giving the address of the register where we want to save the macro. We can tell that we’ve done it right if the word “recording” appears in the status line. Every command that we execute will be captured, right up until we press q again to stop recording.

chapters.title: Matching Patterns and Literals
chapters.summary: The chapter explains how Vim's search engine interprets patterns, beginning with global and per-search case sensitivity and the two regex engines. It contrasts magic, very magic (\v), and very nomagic (\V) searches, then shows captures, backreferences, and noncapturing groups for repeated words and name swapping. The final tips cover word and match boundaries, lookaround assertions, and the /, ?, and \ characters that must still be escaped in search patterns.

Override case sensitivity for one search: \c ignores case, \C forces it.
commands.evidence: We can override Vim’s default case sensitivity using the \c and \C items. Lowercase \c causes the search pattern to ignore case, while the uppercase \C item forces case sensitivity. If either of these items is used in a search pattern, the value of ‘ignorecase’ is overridden for that search.

These search forward and backward, respectively, for the word under the cursor. If we examine the search history after using either of these commands (by pressing /<Up>), we’ll see that the last search pattern is wrapped with word delimiters. Incidentally, the g* and g# variants perform the same searches without word delimiters.

In other words, if our pattern is all lowercase, then the search will be case insensitive. But as soon as we include an uppercase letter, the search becomes case sensitive.

chapters.title: Search
chapters.summary: Chapter 13 is a tour of Vim's search command and the workflows built on it. It covers forward and backward searches with / and ?, repeating with n and N (which inherit direction and offsets), highlighting matches with 'hlsearch' and muting them with :nohlsearch or a <C-l> mapping, previewing matches live with 'incsearch' and completing the search field with <C-r><C-w>, and using search offsets such as /lang/e to land at the end of a match. It then shows how gn enables operating on a complete match (gUgn and the Improved Dot Formula), how to iterate on a pattern through search history or the q/ command-line window, how to count matches with :%s///gn and :vimgrep, and ends with a Vim script that redefines * in Visual mode to search for the current selection.

commands.meaning: Open the forward search prompt; enter a pattern, then press <CR> to execute the search
commands.evidence: From Normal mode, the / key brings up Vim’s search prompt. Here we can enter the pattern, or literal text, that we want to search for. Vim does nothing until we press the <CR> key to execute the search. If we press the <Esc> key instead, the search prompt will be dismissed and we’ll return to Normal mode.

commands.evidence: When a search is initiated with the / key, Vim scans the document forward. If we use the ? key to bring up the search prompt, Vim searches backward instead. The search prompt always begins with either the / or ? character, which indicates in what direction the search will scan.

commands.meaning: Jump to the next match or the previous match for the current search pattern
commands.evidence: The n command jumps to the next match, and the N command jumps to the previous match. We can easily navigate between matches in the current document with the n and N commands. But the definition of “next match” depends on context.

commands.meaning: Move to the next match, then enable Visual mode and select the matching text (also usable as an operator motion)
commands.evidence: When used from Normal mode, gn moves the cursor to the next match, then enables Visual mode and selects the matching text. If your cursor is already on a match, then gn will select the current match without you having to move the cursor. We’ll look at this command in in more detail in Tip 84.

commands.meaning: Mute search highlighting temporarily; it stays muted until the next new or repeat search
commands.evidence: Vim has a more elegant solution. The :nohlsearch command can be used to mute the search highlighting temporarily (see :nohⓘ). It will stay muted until the next time you execute a new or repeat search command. See Create a Shortcut to Mute Highlighting, for a suggested mapping.

My favorite enhancement is enabled with the ‘incsearch’ setting (see 'incsearch'ⓘ). This tells Vim to show a preview of the first match based on what has been entered so far into the search field. Each time we enter another character, Vim instantly updates the preview. This table illustrates how it works:

commands.evidence: Of course, we could simply type out the “carrot” in full. But here’s a handy shortcut: <C-r><C-w>. This autocompletes the search field using the remainder of the current preview match. If we used this command after entering “carr” into the search field, it would append “ot,” causing the match to encompass the entire word “carrot.”

Then, after pressing n a couple of times, we realize that we’d prefer to place the cursor at the end of the match. That’s no problem: we could simply run //e<CR>. When we leave the search field blank like this, Vim reuses the pattern from the previous search. So this repeats the last search but with an offset.

commands.evidence: The gUgn command transforms the matching text to uppercase.

commands.evidence: Instead of pressing /<Up> to prefill the search field with our last pattern, let’s press q/ to summon the command-line window. This acts more or less like a regular Vim buffer, but it’s prepopulated with our search history, one item per line (see Meet the Command-Line Window). We can use the full power of Vim’s modal editing to amend the last pattern.

concepts.evidence: When we execute a search, Vim scans forward from the current cursor position, stopping on the first match that it finds. If nothing is found before the end of the document, Vim informs us “search hit BOTTOM, continuing at TOP.” This means that in some circumstances, a forward search can take us backward. concepts.evidence: Vim records our search patterns so we can easily recall them. When the search prompt is visible, we can scroll through the previous searches by pressing the <Up> key. In fact, the interface for browsing the search history is just the same as for browsing the command-line history. We covered this in more depth in Tip 34. concepts.name: 'hlsearch' highlights every match in the document and in all open splits
concepts.evidence: The search command allows us to jump quickly between matches, but by default, Vim does nothing to make them stand out visually. We can fix this by enabling the ‘hlsearch’ option, (see 'hlsearch'ⓘ), which causes all matches to be highlighted throughout the active document as well as in any other open split windows.

concepts.name: Incremental search gives instant preview feedback before execution
concepts.evidence: This instant feedback lets us know when we’ve hit our target. If our intention was simply to move the cursor to the start of the word “carrot,” then there’s no need to type the full word into the search field. In this case, /carr<CR> is enough. Without the ‘incsearch’ feature enabled, we wouldn’t know whether or not our pattern would hit the target until we executed the search.

concepts.evidence: A search offset can be used to position the cursor a fixed number of characters away from the start or end of a match. In this tip, we’ll study an example where, by placing the cursor at the end of a match, we’re able to complete a series of changes using the Dot Formula.

concepts.evidence: Don’t worry about getting a search pattern right the first time. Vim keeps our most recent search pattern two keystrokes away, so it’s easy to refine a pattern. Start with a broad match; then take as many steps as you need to focus on your target.

chapters.title: Substitution
chapters.summary: Chapter 14, comprising Tips 88 through 97, dissects Vim's :substitute command as an Ex command with a range, a pattern, a replacement string, and optional flags. It shows how the g flag works within a line while a % address works across lines, and how the c flag lets the user confirm each change. Later tips reuse the last search pattern, insert register contents, reference submatches, evaluate Vim script in the replacement field, and finish with project-wide substitutions via :vimgrep and :cfdo.

chapters.title: Global Commands

concepts.name: Quickfix list
concepts.evidence: Vim’s quickfix list is a core feature that allows us to integrate external tools into our workflow. At its simplest, it maintains a sequence of annotated addresses comprising the filename, line number, column number (optional), and a message. Traditionally, these addresses would be a list of error messages generated by a compiler, but they could just as well be warnings from a syntax checker, linter, or any other tool that emits such output.

concepts.name: Edit-compile-edit cycle
concepts.evidence: We get the same result as when we ran make in the shell—except that Vim does something smart with the output. Instead of just echoing the output from make, Vim parses each line, extracting the filename, line number, and error message. For each warning, Vim creates a record in the quickfix list. We can navigate backward and forward through these records, and Vim jumps to the exact line corresponding to the error message. As Vim’s documentation on quickfix says (quickfixⓘ), it allows us to “speed up the edit-compile-edit cycle.”

concepts.name: Jump list recovery with <C-o>

Now suppose that we run :make and immediately realize that we should have used the bang version. How can we get back to where we were before we ran :make? Simple: use the <C-o> command to jump back to the previous position in the jump list. See Tip 56, for more details.

concepts.name: Location list
concepts.evidence: For every command that populates the quickfix list, there’s a variant that places the results in a location list instead. While :make, :grep, and :vimgrep use the quickfix list, :lmake, :lgrep, and :lvimgrep use the location list. So what’s the difference? At any given moment, there can be only one quickfix list, but we can create as many location lists as we want.

concepts.name: Quickfix undo/redo

It explains how generic keyword completion draws on buffers, included files, and tags, how the 'complete' option controls those sources, and how specialized variants complete dictionary words, whole lines, filenames, and context-aware omni suggestions. It also shows how remembered completion context can be reused to insert sequences of words and lines.

concepts.name: SpellBad syntax highlighting marks flagged words
concepts.evidence: The word “Yoru” should now be flagged with the SpellBad syntax highlighting. Typically, that means the word will be underlined with a red dashed line, but how it looks will depend on which color scheme you use.

concepts.name: Separating composition from a final spell-checking pass
concepts.evidence: When writing, I prefer to separate the composition and spell-checking processes into separate tasks. I’ll often disable the spell checker while I write to avoid being nagged each time I make a mistake. Then I’ll make a final pass through the document with the spell checker enabled, fixing the typos it flags.

concepts.name: Buffer-local 'spelllang' option
concepts.evidence: When we enable Vim’s spell checker, it compares words against an English dictionary by default. We can change this by tweaking the ‘spelllang’ option (see 'spelllang'ⓘ). This isn’t a global setting; ‘spelllang’ is always local to the buffer. That means it’s possible to work simultaneously on two or more documents and use a different spell file for each—handy if you’re bilingual.

concepts.name: Regional English spelling variants
concepts.evidence: With this setting, “moustache” would be flagged as a misspelling, but “mustache” would be permitted. Other supported regions include en_au, en_ca, en_gb, and en_nz. See spell-remarksⓘ for more details.

concepts.name: Words added with zg persist across sessions in a spell file
concepts.evidence: Vim records words added to the dictionary in a spell file so that they persist from one session to another. The name of the spell file is derived from the language and file encoding.

concepts.name: 'spellfile' option can hold multiple word lists
concepts.evidence: With the ‘spellfile’ option, we can specify the path of the file where Vim tracks words added or removed using the zg and zw commands (see 'spellfile'ⓘ). Vim allows us to specify more than one spell file simultaneously, which means we can maintain multiple word lists.

concepts.name: Separate spell file for specialist jargon
concepts.evidence: This book contains many strings of text that don’t count as words in English, including Vim commands (such as ciw) and settings (such as ‘spelllang’). I don’t want Vim to keep flagging these as misspelled, but neither do I want to tell Vim to consider them as valid English words. As a compromise, I maintain a separate word list of Vim terminology. I can load this as a spell file any time that I’m writing about Vim.

concepts.name: Count prefix selects which spell file zg writes to
concepts.evidence: For each word that the spell checker flags incorrectly, I now have a choice. I could press 2zg to add it to my list of Vim terminology, or 1zg to add it to the default word list.

concepts.name: Spelling autocompletion without leaving Insert mode
concepts.evidence: Vim’s spelling autocompletion allows us to fix typos without even having to leave Insert mode.

concepts.name: <C-x>s scans backward to the nearest misspelled word
concepts.evidence: When we trigger an autocomplete command, Vim usually offers suggestions on how to complete the word at the current cursor position. But in the case of <C-x>s, Vim scans backward from the cursor position, stopping when it finds a misspelled word. It then builds a word list from suggested corrections and presents them in an autocomplete pop-up menu. We can choose a result using any of the techniques described in Tip 113.

chapters.title: Now What?
chapters.summary: Chapter 21 closes Practical Vim by urging readers to keep practicing until Vim commands become second nature and to pick the book up again, since it is not designed for a single linear pass. It then encourages making Vim your own through a personal vimrc, while insisting that you first learn stock Vim’s baseline behavior—learn to use the saw before sharpening it—and closes with Vim’s charityware license. Note that the assigned range 11753-11976 runs past the chapter body’s end at 11798 into Appendix 1, "Customize Vim to Suit Your Preferences," so the command and concept entries include appendix material.

concepts.name: Shorthand option names
concepts.evidence: Most of Vim’s options also have a shorthand version. The ‘ignorecase’ setting can be abbreviated to ic, so we could toggle this feature by running :se ic! or disable it with :se noic. I tend to use shorthand option names for convenience when customizing Vim on the fly, but I prefer to use the longhand names in my vimrc for the sake of readability.

concepts.name: :setlocal scoping (buffer/window-local options)
concepts.evidence: The :setlocal command scopes the change to the current window or buffer (unless the option can only be set globally). If we were to run :set number, it would enable line numbering for the current window as well as set a new global default. Existing windows would retain their local settings, but new windows would adopt the new global setting.

concepts.name: :source executes each line as an Ex command
concepts.evidence: We can save our customizations by writing them to a file. Then we can use the :source {file} command to apply the settings from the specified {file} to our current editing session (:sourceⓘ). When sourcing a file, Vim executes each line as an Ex command, just as though it had been entered in Command-Line mode.

concepts.name: Autocommands and the FileType event
concepts.evidence: The autocmd declaration tells Vim to listen for an event and to execute the specified commands whenever that event fires (:autocmdⓘ). In this case we’re listening for the FileType event, which is triggered when Vim detects the type of the current file.
